**Other artists whose crossover hits were staples on smooth‑jazz stations (apart from Kenny G and Dave Koz)**  

| Artist | Signature crossover hit(s) that found a place on smooth‑jazz playlists |
|--------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **George Benson** | “Breezin’” (1976) – a smooth‑sax/soft‑pop blend that topped the charts and became a radio‑friendly classic. |
| **Chuck Mangione** | “Feels So Good” (1977) – an easy‑listening flugelhorn tune that crossed over to pop & smooth‑jazz formats. |
| **Bobby Caldwell** | “What You Won’t Do for Love” (1978) – a funky‑R&B ballad that entered smooth‑jazz playlists for its mellow groove. |
| **Spyro Gyra** | “Morning Dance” (1979) – a light‑touch instrumental that bridged jazz fusion with mainstream radio. |
| **Grover Washington Jr. & Bill Withers** | “Just the Two of Us” (1981) – a duet that blended jazz sax with pop‑soul sensibilities, commonly heard on smooth‑jazz stations. |

These are the classic “crossover” acts that the *Smooth Jazz* Wikipedia entry cites as early examples of mainstream hits that were frequently played on smooth‑jazz radio. They—along with Kenny G and Dave Koz—formed the core of the smoothly‑radiated, playlist‑friendly era of smooth jazz.

**Smooth jazz** is a commercially oriented sub-genre style of jazz music that is influenced by R&B, funk, rock and pop music styles (separately, or in any combination).

Beginning in the early-1970s, [jazz fusion] (aka "fusion") was a movement by some jazz musicians to merge the instrumental virtuosity and improvisation of traditional jazz, with a modern, electronic sensibility. The instrument that has become the most widely-associated with the genre is the saxophone inspired by players like [Grover Washington Jr.], [Ronnie Laws], [Wayne Shorter] and [Nathan Davis] "Nathan Davis (saxophonist)"); plus a gentle, [legato][electric guitar] (influenced by players like [Wes Montgomery] and [Grant Green]). Jazz fusion ensembles such as [Weather Report], [Spyro Gyra], [Hiroshima] "Hiroshima (band)") and [Bob James' Fourplay] "Bob James (musician)") were vital to the development of the genre.

Modern derivatives of the genre includes the more recent New Adult Contemporary format broadcast radio. "Smooth jazz" has been successful as a radio format, particularly in the 1980s and 1990s; however, its popularity has been on a decline since the 2000s, and most radio play today takes place on non-commercial radio stations.[_[citation needed]_]

## Description

[[edit]]

In general, a smooth jazz track is downtempo (the most widely played tracks are in the 90–105 BPM range), layering a lead, melody-playing instrument (saxophones – especially soprano and tenor – are the most popular with guitars a close second) over a backdrop that typically consists of programmed rhythms and various pads and/or samples.

Smooth jazz groups or recording artists tend to play their instruments in a melodic fashion such that they are recognizable within just a few measures; this category includes names such as saxophonists [Kenny G], [Najee], [David Sanborn], [George Howard] "George Howard (jazz)") and [Art Porter Jr.]; guitarists [George Benson], [Earl Klugh], [Marc Antoine] "Marc Antoine (musician)"), [Peter White] "Peter White (musician)"), [Jonathan Butler], [Norman Brown] "Norman Brown (guitarist)"), [Ronny Jordan], and [Yves Vincent]; keyboardist/pianists [Joe Sample], [David Benoit], and [Bradley Joseph]. Some performers, such as [Dave Koz], Bob James, and [Nathan East] are notable for their numerous collaborations with many of the genre's big names. Groups include [Fourplay], [Pieces of a Dream] "Pieces of a Dream (band)"), [Acoustic Alchemy], [Airbourne] "Airbourne (band)") and [the Rippingtons]. Female performers includes [Keiko Matsui], [Joyce Cooling], [Mindi Abair], [Candy Dulfer], [Sade] "Sade (band)"), [Brenda Russell], [Pamela Williams], [Regina Belle] and [Anita Baker].

## History

[[edit]]

Smooth jazz may be thought of as commercially-oriented, crossover jazz which came to prominence in the 1980s, displacing the more venturesome [jazz fusion] from which it emerged. It avoids the [improvisational] "risk-taking" of jazz fusion, emphasizing melodic form, and much of the music was initially "a combination of jazz with easy-listening [pop music] and lightweight [R&B]."[[1]][[2]]

During the mid-1970s in the United States, it was known as "smooth radio"; the genre was not termed "smooth jazz" until the 1980s.[[3]]

The term itself seems to have been birthed directly out of radio marketing efforts. In an industry focus group in the late 1980s, one participant coined the phrase "smooth jazz" – and it stuck.[[4]][[5]]

The popularity of smooth jazz as a radio format grew in the '80s and '90s, but gradually declined in the early 2000s. By 2009, many stations including in NYC, Washington, DC, and Boston had switched away from the format.[[6]]

Smooth jazz grew in popularity in the 1980s and 1990s as [Anita Baker], [Sade] "Sade (singer)"), [Al Jarreau], [Grover Washington Jr.] and [Kenny G] released multiple hit songs.[[7]]
